implementation_notes: Default realization: open one sqlx transaction (pool.begin()) and, inside it, lock the aggregate root row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, then read and write members through the same executor; the row lock lives until commit or rollback, so it spans processes and hosts. The type system enforces the mechanics you would otherwise document - the Transaction is not Send/'static, so it cannot accidentally outlive its scope or be shared across tasks, which replaces the classic lock manager and its release bookkeeping.

variants.idiom_name: sqlx::Transaction + SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the root
pitfalls: The borrow checker will not let the transaction be shared across tasks, and the sqlx pool does not pin a connection: never re-acquire from the pool inside the cluster edit, or the member writes run outside the lock.
A transaction held across user think time keeps a pooled connection and the row lock; use a version token (UPDATE ... WHERE version = ...) for long sessions.

variants.name: Mutex guard owns the whole aggregate
variants.implementation_notes: In-process realization: put the cluster behind one Mutex<Aggregate> and let its guard be the lock - accessing root and members is only possible through the guard, so per-member locking and lock ordering disappear and the borrow checker proves exclusivity. std::sync::Mutex documents exactly this: the data can only be accessed through the RAII guards returned by lock/try_lock. It coordinates one process only, and poisoning means a panic inside the guard typically has to be surfaced rather than ignored.
pitfalls: Poisoning: if a thread panics while holding the guard, later lock() calls return Err and unwrap panics in turn - decide explicitly whether to propagate or recover.
Guards are not Send across await points in async code (std Mutex is not async-aware); use a tokio::sync::Mutex or scope the guard so it never spans an await.
